concept.title: Dates
concept.shortdesc: How uFTi records a date, from one you know in full to one you only know in part.

conbody.p: Most dates are simple. Type the day, the month and the year, such as 15 March 1900. You can write the month in words or choose it from the list.
A line under the date starts with Reads as. It shows how uFTi has understood the date. Look at it each time. If it is not what you meant, change the date.

section.title: When you know less
section.p: The date editor asks . Choose , or , to match what the record gives you.
Do not make up a day or a month to fill the gap. A newspaper may say that a book came out in December 1847. Then choose the month and the year, and stop there.

section.title: When you are not sure
section.p: Choose to say how sure you are. You can say that a date is about right, worked out by you, or a limit. You can also give a span of time. lists each choice, with an example.

section.title: Typing the date
section.p: Choose to type the whole date in one box, such as about 1900 or between 1850 and 1860. Some things you might type are kept as typed and not read as a date. says which.

section.title: Old dates
section.p: A date from long ago may need more care. Britain changed its calendar in 1752. Before that, the year there began in March. uFTi can keep a date in the calendar of the record. explains how, and works through a real case.

section.title: Where dates are used
section.p: uFTi uses dates to order the events of a person. shows where you can enter a date, how dates are shown and how uncertain dates are ordered.
